Consider CATERING_ORDER (booking_ref, booking_date, client_no, client_name, client_city, dish_code, dish_name, dish_style, dish_price, portions), where the primary key is booking_ref + dish_code.

What kind of dependency is dish_code → dish_name?
options: A full functional dependency on the primary key
questions.explanation: dish_code is only half of the composite key, so anything it determines on its own is partially dependent.

questions.question: In CATERING_ORDER (PK = booking_ref + dish_code), what kind of dependency is (booking_ref, dish_code) → portions?
options: A full functional dependency on the whole primary key
questions.explanation: How many portions of a dish were ordered depends on which dish AND which booking — you need the whole key, so it's fully functionally dependent and stays put.

questions.question: In CATERING_ORDER (PK = booking_ref + dish_code), client_no depends on booking_ref, and client_name depends on client_no. What is client_name's relationship to booking_ref?
options: A full functional dependency on the composite key
questions.explanation: booking_ref → client_no → client_name. Because client_no is not a key attribute, that chain is a transitive dependency.

questions.question: In CATERING_ORDER, which set of attributes should move into a DISH table when you convert to 2NF?
questions.explanation: Everything determined by dish_code alone travels with it, and dish_code becomes the new table's primary key. portions stays behind — it needs both halves of the key.

questions.question: After splitting CATERING_ORDER into 2NF, one table is BOOKING (booking_ref, booking_date, client_no, client_name, client_city). Why is this still not in 3NF?
options: client_name and client_city depend on client_no, which is not the primary key
questions.explanation: A transitive dependency. Splitting out CLIENT (client_no, client_name, client_city) and leaving client_no behind as a foreign key gets you to 3NF.

questions.question: SEMINAR_ROSTER (seminar_code, seminar_title, room_code, room_capacity, attendee_id, attendee_name, grade) has primary key seminar_code + attendee_id. Which is a TRANSITIVE dependency?
questions.explanation: room_code is not part of the key, and it determines room_capacity — a dependency between two nonprime attributes. The first two options are partial dependencies; the last is a proper full dependency.

questions.question: In SEMINAR_ROSTER (PK = seminar_code + attendee_id), which attribute is fully functionally dependent on the whole key?
questions.explanation: A grade belongs to one attendee in one seminar, so it needs both halves. Everything else depends on just one part, or on a nonprime attribute.

questions.question: A repeating group in a table looks like:
options: Several columns holding the same kind of fact — phone1, phone2, phone3 — or several values crammed into one cell
Two rows with the same primary key
A foreign key that appears twice
A column with the same value in every row
questions.explanation: Either shape breaks 1NF. Both are fixed the same way: move the repeating fact into its own table, one row per value.

questions.question: A TRAIL_PERMIT table stores a column trail_codes containing values like 'RID-2, LKE-7, SUM-1'. Which normal form does this violate, and how is it fixed?
options: 1NF — split the repeating group into its own table, one row per trail
It violates nothing; the values are comma-separated for efficiency
questions.explanation: Multiple values in one cell is a repeating group, which breaks 1NF and the atomic attribute rule. It is the same mistake as stuffing several key values into one foreign key field.

questions.question: ______ deliberately produces a lower normal form, increasing performance at the cost of greater data redundancy.
questions.explanation: Denormalization. It is a considered trade-off, not an accident.

questions.question: Why might a designer choose to denormalize?
options: To increase performance, accepting greater redundancy in return
Because 3NF is not a valid design
To remove the need for primary keys
questions.explanation: More tables mean more I/O operations and more processing logic to join them, so there is a real cost to normalizing.

questions.question: More tables require more I/O operations and processing logic to join them.
questions.explanation: Which is why it also says normalization is important, but only part of the design process.

questions.question: A table is in 3NF but one of its determinants is not a candidate key. Which normal form does it fail?
questions.explanation: BCNF requires every determinant to be a candidate key. It is a special case of 3NF.

questions.question: Match each problem to the normal form that fixes it.

pairs.left: A cell holding several values at once
pairs.right: 1NF

pairs.left: An attribute determined by half of a composite key
pairs.right: 2NF

pairs.left: An attribute determined by another non-key attribute
pairs.right: 3NF

pairs.left: A determinant that is not a candidate key
pairs.right: BCNF

questions.explanation: Reading a dependency diagram left to right, these are the four faults you're hunting for, in the order you fix them.

questions.question: Normalization is the whole of database design.
questions.explanation: Normalization is important, but only part of the design process.

questions.question:
CATERING_ORDER is in 1NF with the following columns:

  booking_ref, booking_date, client_no, client_name, client_city,
  dish_code, dish_name, dish_style, dish_price, portions

The primary key is booking_ref + dish_code.

Write the complete dependency set for the table as it stands in 1NF — the full dependency on the whole key, every partial dependency, and every transitive dependency.
questions.modelAnswer:
Full functional dependency on the whole primary key:
  (booking_ref, dish_code) → portions

Partial dependencies:
  booking_ref → booking_date, client_no, client_name, client_city
  dish_code   → dish_name, dish_style, dish_price

Transitive dependency:
  client_no → client_name, client_city

Read it as: how many portions were ordered needs both halves of the key; everything about the booking follows from booking_ref alone; everything about the dish follows from dish_code alone; and the client's name and city follow from client_no, which is itself just an ordinary attribute of the booking.
rubric: Identified (booking_ref, dish_code) → portions as the only full dependency on the whole key
Listed booking_ref → booking_date, client_no, client_name, client_city as a partial dependency
Listed dish_code → dish_name, dish_style, dish_price as a partial dependency
Identified client_no → client_name, client_city as the transitive dependency
questions.explanation: Work in this order every time: what needs the whole key, what needs only part of it, and what hangs off a non-key attribute. That ordering is the dependency set.

questions.question:
Continuing with CATERING_ORDER (booking_ref, booking_date, client_no, client_name, client_city, dish_code, dish_name, dish_style, dish_price, portions), primary key booking_ref + dish_code.

Write the 2NF relational schemas — the tables you get after removing the partial dependencies. Underline or otherwise mark the primary key of each.
questions.modelAnswer:
BOOKING (booking_ref [PK], booking_date, client_no, client_name, client_city)

DISH (dish_code [PK], dish_name, dish_style, dish_price)

BOOKING_LINE (booking_ref [PK, FK], dish_code [PK, FK], portions)

Each partial dependency became its own table, keyed on its determinant. What remains in BOOKING_LINE is the original composite key plus the one attribute that genuinely needed both halves of it — portions. The two key columns are now foreign keys back to BOOKING and DISH.

This is 2NF, not yet 3NF: BOOKING still carries the transitive dependency client_no → client_name, client_city.
rubric: Produced three tables
Keyed BOOKING on booking_ref and DISH on dish_code
Kept portions in the linking table with the composite key (booking_ref, dish_code)
Marked the composite key columns as foreign keys as well as the primary key
Noted that this is still only 2NF because a transitive dependency remains
questions.explanation: The mechanical rule: each partial dependency's determinant becomes a new table's primary key, and everything it determined goes with it.

questions.question: Finish the job on CATERING_ORDER. Write the 3NF relational schemas, marking the primary key and any foreign keys in each table.
questions.modelAnswer:
CLIENT (client_no [PK], client_name, client_city)

BOOKING (booking_ref [PK], booking_date, client_no [FK to CLIENT])

DISH (dish_code [PK], dish_name, dish_style, dish_price)

BOOKING_LINE (booking_ref [PK, FK to BOOKING], dish_code [PK, FK to DISH], portions)

The move from 2NF to 3NF was the first two tables: the transitive dependency client_no → client_name, client_city came out of BOOKING into its own CLIENT table, and client_no stayed behind in BOOKING as the foreign key linking them.

Now every non-key attribute in every table depends on the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key.
rubric: Produced four tables
Created CLIENT keyed on client_no, holding client_name and client_city
Left client_no in BOOKING as a foreign key
Left DISH and BOOKING_LINE unchanged from 2NF
Marked primary and foreign keys throughout
questions.explanation: "The key, the whole key, and nothing but the key" is a compact test: nothing but the key catches transitive dependencies, and the whole key catches partial ones.

questions.question:
SEMINAR_ROSTER is in 1NF:

  seminar_code, seminar_title, room_code, room_capacity,
  attendee_id, attendee_name, attendee_email, grade

The primary key is seminar_code + attendee_id. Each seminar meets in exactly one room.

Write the complete dependency set for this table in 1NF.
questions.modelAnswer:
Full functional dependency on the whole primary key:
  (seminar_code, attendee_id) → grade

Partial dependencies:
  seminar_code → seminar_title, room_code, room_capacity
  attendee_id  → attendee_name, attendee_email

Transitive dependency:
  room_code → room_capacity

Only the grade needs both halves of the key: it is one person's mark in one seminar. Room capacity is listed twice above deliberately — it follows from seminar_code by way of room_code, and the room_code → room_capacity link is what makes it transitive.
rubric: Identified (seminar_code, attendee_id) → grade as the only full dependency
Listed seminar_code → seminar_title, room_code, room_capacity
Listed attendee_id → attendee_name, attendee_email
Identified room_code → room_capacity as the transitive dependency
questions.explanation: Two partial dependencies, one from each half of the composite key, plus one transitive dependency hanging off a nonprime attribute — the same shape as the catering example.

questions.question: Write the 3NF relational schemas for SEMINAR_ROSTER (seminar_code, seminar_title, room_code, room_capacity, attendee_id, attendee_name, attendee_email, grade), primary key seminar_code + attendee_id, where each seminar meets in exactly one room.
questions.modelAnswer:
ROOM (room_code [PK], room_capacity)

SEMINAR (seminar_code [PK], seminar_title, room_code [FK to ROOM])

ATTENDEE (attendee_id [PK], attendee_name, attendee_email)

ENROLLMENT (seminar_code [PK, FK to SEMINAR], attendee_id [PK, FK to ATTENDEE], grade)

The two partial dependencies became SEMINAR and ATTENDEE; the transitive dependency became ROOM, with room_code left behind in SEMINAR as the foreign key. ENROLLMENT keeps the composite key and the single attribute that needed all of it.

ENROLLMENT is a bridge table — the M:N between seminars and attendees, resolved.
rubric: Produced four tables
Split ROOM out with room_code as its primary key
Left room_code in SEMINAR as a foreign key
Kept grade in a linking table keyed on (seminar_code, attendee_id)
Marked both linking columns as foreign keys
questions.explanation: Worth noticing: normalizing an M:N-shaped table produces exactly the bridge entity you would have drawn on the ERD. The two techniques agree.

questions.question: Explain the practical difference between a partial dependency and a transitive dependency: how you spot each one, and which anomaly each one causes.
questions.modelAnswer:
A partial dependency is a non-key attribute determined by only PART of a composite primary key. You spot it by covering up half the key and asking whether the attribute is still determined — if dish_code alone tells you dish_price, dish_price is partially dependent. It can only exist when the key is composite. The anomaly: the dish's price is repeated on every order line for that dish, so changing it means changing many rows, and a dish nobody has ordered yet cannot be recorded at all.

A transitive dependency is a non-key attribute determined by ANOTHER non-key attribute. You spot it by looking for a chain among ordinary attributes — booking_ref determines client_no, and client_no determines client_name. Neither side of client_no → client_name is part of the key. The anomaly: the client's details are repeated on every booking they make, and deleting their last booking erases the client entirely.

Both are fixed the same way: move the determinant and everything it determines into a new table, and leave the determinant behind as a foreign key.
rubric: Defined partial dependency as determined by part of a composite key
Defined transitive dependency as determined by another non-key attribute
Noted that a partial dependency requires a composite primary key
Named a concrete anomaly caused by each
Said both are fixed by splitting the determinant into its own table with a foreign key left behind
questions.explanation: If you can state the fix in one sentence — new table keyed on the determinant, foreign key left behind — you can normalize anything you're given.

questions.question: A classmate says: "My table has a single-column primary key, so I skipped 2NF and went straight to checking 3NF." Are they right? Explain.
questions.modelAnswer:
Yes, they are right, and for the correct reason. A partial dependency means an attribute is determined by part of the primary key. A single-column primary key has no proper parts, so no partial dependency can exist. Any table in 1NF with a simple key is therefore already in 2NF, and going straight to hunting for transitive dependencies is legitimate.

What they must not skip is the 3NF check itself. A single-column key gives no protection at all against a chain like booking_ref → client_no → client_name, which is exactly the kind of dependency 3NF exists to remove.
rubric: Agreed that they are right
Explained that a partial dependency needs part of a composite key, and a one-column key has no parts
Concluded that such a table is automatically in 2NF
Warned that the 3NF check still matters, because transitive dependencies are unaffected
questions.explanation: Worth internalizing: composite key means look for partial dependencies; any key at all means look for transitive ones.
